caption:
Amazon is working on a plan to collect data on nearly every product sold worldwide, even ones it does not stock, Reuters reports.
An internal document says it would crawl other retailers' sites and take data straight from brands like Coca-Cola and Bayer.
The goal: keep shoppers on Amazon as AI agents like Meta's Muse start buying for them.

Would you let an AI agent shop for you instead of opening Amazon?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Reuters · Photo: Amazon

paragraphs.text: Amazon has drafted a plan to collect data on nearly every product sold worldwide, including products it does not carry, according to an internal document reviewed by Reuters and reported on November 13, 2026. The initiative is called World Product Graph, and the document describing it lists October 1, 2027 as an aspirational release date.

The document is a PR/FAQ, the roughly six-page memo format Amazon uses to pitch new projects. Reuters said it could not determine whether or when the plan will be carried out, and that it could be changed or dropped for financial or other reasons. Amazon told the news agency that draft and outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and that the document does not necessarily reflect its current plans.
How the World Product Graph would work

According to Reuters, the plan depends on learning how brands organize products on their own websites. That would come from data contributed directly by brands and from independent crawling of other retailers' sites. Reuters could not determine how the crawling would work or whether Amazon would seek permission. The document says Coca-Cola and Bayer have signed up to contribute data, and mentions a CEO-level summit with Procter & Gamble for a trial. None of the three companies responded to Reuters.

The project sits in Amazon's Selection & Catalog Systems unit and is organized under Vice President Robert Tekiela, who did not respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported. Employees describe it as an expansion of Buy for Me and Shop Direct, two features that let customers buy products sold on other websites through Amazon.

The document also argues that Amazon cannot be the main destination for every shopping trip if customers have to leave the site to research products. Reuters cited a 2025 Morgan Stanley study that found 57% of online shoppers start product research on Google and 16% on Amazon, although 41% start on Amazon when they already know what they want.
The pressure from AI shopping agents

The plan comes as AI agents that search and buy on a shopper's behalf spread. Meta's Muse agent has gained more than 10 million users in the United States and Canada since its September launch, according to Reuters, and Amazon blocked it from its retail site that month. Amazon also blocked xAI's Grok agent, and it sued Perplexity last year to stop similar access; that case is ongoing.

In public, Amazon has played down the threat. On the company's third quarter earnings call, chief executive Andy Jassy said few customers were doing much shopping through such agents yet. People familiar with the matter told Reuters that executives are more worried than they have said publicly.

The internal document also criticizes Amazon's own AI shopping assistant. It says Rufus, which Amazon folded into a new brand called Alexa for Shopping in May 2026, often gives wrong or incomplete answers, and that handling about 83 million searches a week is expensive. Amazon said those usage figures are significantly outdated and that Alexa for Shopping gives correct answers about 97% of the time worldwide.

Alexa for Shopping combines the Rufus chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant across Amazon's apps, website and Echo devices, GeekWire reported, and it is free for signed-in Amazon customers in the United States. Amazon has said Rufus was used by more than 300 million customers in 2025.

The plan shows where Amazon sees the risk. If shoppers ask an AI agent to compare products across the web, the agent becomes the storefront, and Amazon becomes one supplier among many. A catalog that covers products Amazon does not sell would let its own assistant answer those questions first, and crawling rival retailers to build it could invite the same kind of objections Amazon has raised against agents that access its own site.
The key signal is whether Amazon confirms World Product Graph publicly, and whether brands beyond Coca-Cola and Bayer agree to send product data before the 2027 target date.
